hints: Focus on solubility, not just the reaction type. Ask yourself for each step whether the magnesium or barium product formed is soluble or insoluble in water.
Work through the magnesium row first. Carbonate gives MgCO3 and hydroxide gives Mg(OH)2, both are white precipitates, while the chloride after acid is soluble.
Now compare barium to magnesium for the last step. Remember solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group, so think about whether Ba(OH)2 will precipitate like Mg(OH)2 does.
walkthrough:
**Identify M and Q from carbonate addition**

Both $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ give insoluble carbonates with sodium carbonate. So M is $\text{MgCO}_3$ and Q is $\text{BaCO}_3$, both white precipitates.

$$\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + \text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCO}_3(s)$$
$$\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaCO}_3(s)$$

**Add excess HCl and boil to get N and R**

Acid dissolves the carbonates to give soluble chlorides plus $\text{CO}_2$. Boiling drives off dissolved $\text{CO}_2$.

$$\text{MgCO}_3(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2(aq) + \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
$$\text{BaCO}_3(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaCl}_2(aq) + \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
So N is $\text{MgCl}_2(aq)$ and R is $\text{BaCl}_2(aq)$. Neither is a precipitate.

**Add excess NaOH to get P and S**

This is where Mg and Ba behave differently. Magnesium hydroxide is insoluble, but barium hydroxide is soluble.

$$\text{MgCl}_2(aq) + 2\text{NaOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) + 2\text{NaCl}(aq)$$
$$\text{BaCl}_2(aq) + 2\text{NaOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Ba(OH)}_2(aq) + 2\text{NaCl}(aq)$$
So P is white precipitate $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, while S stays in solution.

**Count the white precipitates**

M (white ppt) + P (white ppt) + Q (white ppt) = 3 precipitates. N, R and S are all soluble aqueous solutions. That gives a total of 3.

options.A: 2 is too low. It correctly counts M and P or M and Q, but misses the key difference. Both MgCO3, Mg(OH)2 and BaCO3 are white precipitates, giving 3 in total.
options.B: 3 is correct. M = MgCO3(s) white ppt, P = Mg(OH)2(s) white ppt, Q = BaCO3(s) white ppt. N = MgCl2(aq), R = BaCl2(aq) and S = Ba(OH)2(aq) are all soluble, so they are not precipitates.
options.C: 4 is incorrect. This often comes from assuming S = Ba(OH)2 is a white precipitate like Mg(OH)2. In fact Group 2 hydroxide solubility increases down the group, so Ba(OH)2 is soluble and no precipitate forms.
options.D: 5 is incorrect. This comes from assuming the chlorides N and R are precipitates. All Group 2 chlorides and all nitrates are soluble, and excess HCl dissolves the carbonates completely, so N and R are solutions.
